sender.en: “Australian Federal Police” and then your “crypto exchange”

name.en: Fake AFP call: “a cybercrime report was made in your name”, move your crypto

how.en: Scammers pretending to be the AFP or state police call crypto owners and say they were caught up in a data breach. They have already filed a fake ReportCyber report with your stolen details, so you get a real-looking email and reference number. They ask you to confirm a one-time PIN. A second scammer then calls as your crypto exchange, quotes the same reference and asks for your seed phrase or tells you to move your crypto to a “cold storage” account.

text.en: A caller says they are from the AFP or police and that you were in a crypto data breach.
They say a ReportCyber report was lodged in your name and ask you to confirm the one-time PIN in your email.
A second caller says they are from your crypto exchange and gives the same reference number.
They ask for your seed phrase or tell you to move your crypto to a “cold storage” wallet.

This is the Australian Federal Police cybercrime unit. Your details were found in a data breach involving your cryptocurrency account. A report has been lodged for you through ReportCyber. Please read me the one-time PIN we just emailed you to confirm it.

en: A call from “police” about your crypto or a data breach.
Emails from ReportCyber about a report you didn’t make.
Being asked to read out a one-time PIN.
Being asked for your seed phrase or to move crypto to keep it safe.
Hang up. Police won’t ask you to move crypto or share codes.
Never share your seed phrase or one-time PIN with anyone.
If you lost crypto, contact your exchange straight away and report to police through ReportCyber, giving the fake reference number.
